transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Since my wife and I separated, I’ve felt this heavy, empty mood that I can’t shake, even when I’m at the library or around art. My niece noticed how much I've changed lately and convinced me to come in and speak to someone.
Did these symptoms start soon after your separation, and do they feel mainly tied to that event, or have you had similar depressive episodes at other times in your life even without a major stressor?

This current heavy spell started about three months ago when the separation became official and I moved into my own apartment. But looking back, these cycles of dragging lows and revved-up stretches have actually been coming and going for many years. They've just gotten much more intense and noticeable over the past year as my marriage fell apart.

During those revved-up stretches, did you need much less sleep and feel unusually energetic or confident, talking more than usual or doing risky things? About how long did those periods typically last?

Yes, I'd only sleep three or four hours but wake up buzzing, feeling so confident that I thought I could easily run the whole library branch. I would talk incredibly fast, jumping from topic to topic, and though I didn't do risky things, I'd throw myself into too many projects at once. These high-energy stretches usually last for a few days at a time and have been coming and going for many years.

During those high-energy periods, did other people clearly notice you were acting unusually different, and did those periods ever cause major problems at work, require hospitalization, or include feeling out of touch with reality?

Yes, people definitely noticed—my niece would tease me for talking too fast, and coworkers saw me cracking jokes or sometimes snapping over small things. But those high periods never caused major disasters, required hospital stays, or made me lose touch with reality; they just felt like highly productive, intense bursts. It's actually this current low spell that is causing me to struggle and fall behind at work.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports many years of recurrent mood cycling with distinct periods of elevated energy, decreased need for sleep, inflated confidence, increased talkativeness, racing/jumping thoughts, and increased goal-directed activity lasting a few days, noticed by others but without psychosis, hospitalization, or marked impairment during the highs—consistent with hypomanic episodes. He also currently has a significant depressive episode causing occupational impairment. This pattern is most consistent with bipolar affective disorder with hypomanic and depressive episodes, without evidence of full mania.
